title: OCR-Anchor Reranking: When Best-of-N Selection Fails Due to Candidate Homogeneity

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
The purpose of the contribution is to improve document-OCR outputs of vision-language models (VLMs) by selecting the best among multiple VLM-generated parsing candidates without retraining. This specific purpose is not directly addressed by any prior paper. While [3] discusses post-OCR error correction by reconciling multiple OCR views, it focuses on reducing errors in OCR outputs using language models, not on selecting the best parsing candidate from VLM outputs. Similarly, [1] and [6] address challenges in document understanding and OCR capabilities of VLMs but do not focus on selecting the best parsing candidate. No prior paper explicitly shares the same purpose.

### Mechanism
The mechanism involves a training-free method, OCR-Anchor Reranking, which extracts high-confidence anchor tokens from a classical OCR engine (PaddleOCR) and selects the VLM candidate with the highest fraction of anchor-token coverage. [4] proposes an anchor-based pairwise comparison for reranking in recommendation systems, which is conceptually similar in using anchors for reranking. However, [4] applies this mechanism to recommendation systems, not OCR or VLM parsing. Despite the domain difference, the underlying primitive of anchor-based reranking is substantively equivalent. Therefore, the mechanism is covered by [4].

### Evaluation
The evaluation design involves comparing the proposed method against a single-sample baseline. This is a standard evaluation design and does not introduce a new benchmark, metric, or protocol. [4] evaluates its anchor-based reranking method using a similar comparative design, albeit in the recommendation domain. Additionally, [9] and [13] also evaluate reranking methods using comparative designs. Thus, the evaluation design is covered by prior work.

### Domain
The domain is document OCR and VLM-based PDF-to-Markdown parsing. This falls under the broader area of document understanding and OCR, which is addressed by [1], [6], [10], and [11]. These papers work on improving OCR and document understanding using VLMs or related methods. While the specific task of PDF-to-Markdown parsing may not be explicitly addressed, it is a sub-problem within the established domain of document OCR. Therefore, the domain is covered.

The purpose combines: (1) improving VLM OCR output quality, and (2) doing so via candidate selection (reranking) without retraining. Paper [3] addresses "post-OCR correction" using multiple OCR views to reduce errors, but focuses on combining views rather than selecting among VLM candidates. Paper [1] (DocVLM) improves VLM document understanding but via architectural changes, not selection. Paper [2] is a training-free reranker for RAG, not OCR output improvement. The purpose-level objective — training-free best-candidate selection to improve output quality — is substantively present in [2].

**MECHANISM: OCR-Anchor Reranking — extract high-confidence tokens from a classical OCR engine, use coverage of those anchor tokens to score and select among VLM candidates.**

This is a specific primitive: use a trusted external signal (classical OCR high-confidence tokens) as anchors to score candidates by coverage. Paper [4] uses "anchor-based pairwise comparison" for recommendation reranking, but anchors there are reference items in a list, not external-signal tokens. Paper [3] uses multiple OCR views and a language model to reconcile them — different primitive (LM scoring, not anchor-token coverage). Paper [18] uses "translation consensus between decoders" — n-gram agreement to rerank, which is structurally similar (shared tokens across outputs used as signal), but the anchor comes from within the candidate set, not from an external trusted source. Paper [19] (consensus decoding) similarly uses agreement among hypotheses. None of these use an *external* classical system's high-confidence outputs as anchor tokens to score VLM candidates by coverage. This mechanism appears genuinely absent.

The evaluation design here is essentially: propose a method, run it on a benchmark, compare against a baseline (single-sample), and report that it fails to improve. This is a standard ablation/comparison experimental design. Papers like [27] (MBR decoding properties, empirical evaluation against baselines) and [3] use standard benchmark comparisons. However, per the special rule, generic experimental moves don't establish coverage unless they validate the same claim with a named benchmark/metric family. The evaluation here seems to use document parsing quality metrics (likely CER/WER or similar OCR metrics), which appear in [3] and [10]. Paper [3] uses standard OCR error metrics to compare multi-view correction against baselines. This design (OCR quality metric comparison against baseline) is covered by [3].

**DOMAIN: Document OCR / VLM-based PDF-to-Markdown parsing.**

Paper [1] (DocVLM) works in document understanding with VLMs. Paper [6] (Ocean-OCR) works in OCR with VLMs. Paper [11] (FireRed-OCR) specializes VLMs for document OCR. Paper [10] (TrOCR) is transformer-based OCR. These all operate in the document OCR / VLM document understanding area. Domain is clearly covered by [1], [6], [10], [11].
